overview: This record follows Congo-Kinshasa, the Democratic Republic of the Congo, from the late colonial period into independence. Zaire was its name from 1971 to 1997; it is a different state from neighboring Congo-Brazzaville.

periods.title: Late Belgian colonial rule
periods.summary: The imported record begins before independence on 30 June 1960.

periods.title: Independence, dictatorship and Zaire
periods.summary: Political crisis followed independence; decades of Mobutu’s rule ended during the first Congo War.

periods.title: Restored name and continuing state
periods.summary: The name Democratic Republic of the Congo returned in 1997.

items.text: The successive names Congo-Leopoldville, Democratic Republic of the Congo and Zaire do not identify three vanished populations. The UN’s country-name record tracks changes in official terminology. Keeping the dates straight also prevents confusion with the separate Republic of the Congo across the river.

The independence crisis brought the first UN peacekeeping operation in 1960. Later wars in 1996 to 1997 and 1998 to 2003 involved regional forces and armed groups. The UN’s 2025 history describes continuing violence and displacement, a serious part of modern life alongside cultural achievement.

Article 1 of the constitution, in its 2011 edition, prints the motto “Justice - Paix - Travail”: “Justice - Peace - Work”. This is a short attested French writing sample. The same article recognizes Kikongo, Lingala, Swahili and Tshiluba as national languages, showing that official French is only part of the linguistic picture.

sections.title: Music and cities imagined in miniature

items.text: Congolese rumba belongs to communities in both Congo states and their diaspora. Musicians perform it at celebrations and in mourning, in homes, public spaces and religious settings. Its social life extends far beyond the concert stage or a famous recording.

Younger musicians learn through neighborhood clubs, schools and community organizations. Established performers train apprentices in playing and making instruments. A musical tradition survives through rehearsal, teaching and practical work as well as moments when an audience gets up to dance.

Kinshasa-based artist Bodys Isek Kingelez built dazzling architectural models from paper, packaging, plastic, cans and bottle caps. Everyday discarded materials became towers and public spaces. His creations ask viewers to imagine how cities might serve people better.

In Kimbembele Ihunga, made in 1994, Kingelez reimagined his home village with a stadium, banks, restaurants and skyscrapers. Ville Fantome, from 1996, pictured a peaceful city that needed neither police nor doctors. These were artistic hopes, not claims that real communities had solved every problem.

An IITA project launched in 2023 sought to strengthen cassava growing and processing in the DRC, including flour for breadmaking. The plan linked farmers, processors and bakeries. A familiar crop could become part of an effort to reduce dependence on imported wheat.

The cassava project also addressed processing and access to buyers. Growing a crop is only one part of getting food onto a household table: roots must reach the right place in usable condition, and farmers need customers as well as harvests.

At Chirhavanyi Primary School in Walungu, a new water supply and hygienic toilets arrived in 2021. Fourteen-year-old Asifiwe later described being able to wash her hands at school. An ordinary school break no longer needed to revolve around finding water.

At nearby Izenge Health Centre, Chinama described previously leaving her sick daughter to fetch water far away. A water point close to the rooms changed that task. Infrastructure matters at the scale of one parent trying to care for one child, as well as in national statistics.

Doctor Denis Mukwege shared the 2018 Nobel Peace Prize for work against sexual violence in war. At Panzi Hospital in Bukavu, his team cared for injured women and girls. Their achievement joined skilled medicine with advocacy for survivors’ dignity and protection.

ending.text: The state continued after the end of Mobutu’s regime and the name Zaire in 1997. Subsequent wars and continuing armed violence did not erase Congolese communities, institutions or creative life.
